meta.date: ~559–545 BC (engraved); the burden dated to the year Ahaz died, ~715 BC

world_behind.title: The block's last chapter
world_behind.text: Thirteen chapters of Isaiah end here, and Nephi resumes in his own voice immediately afterward. Whatever he intended by the selection, this is where he chose to stop, and the chapter's final line is about Zion founded and the poor trusting in it.

world_behind.title: A funeral song for a living king
world_behind.text: Verses 4 through 21 are a taunt in the form of a lament, the shape used at a royal burial, sung over a king who has not yet fallen. Ancient hearers would have recognized the genre immediately, and the recognition is the joke: the ceremony is being rehearsed early.

world_behind.title: Cedars that talk
world_behind.text: In verse 8 the trees of Lebanon speak, relieved that no woodcutter comes up any more. Assyrian and Babylonian kings recorded logging expeditions to Lebanon for palace timber. The trees are celebrating the end of a specific imperial practice, not making a general point about nature.

world_behind.title: The mount of the congregation
world_behind.text: Verse 13 names a northern mountain where the gods were thought to assemble in the older mythology of the region. The boast quoted there is not vague ambition; it is a claim to a specific seat, which is what makes the answer in verse 15 so exact: not that seat, but the pit.

world_behind.title: Unburied
world_behind.text: Verses 18 through 20 turn on a practice rather than an image: kings of the nations lie in glory, each in his own tomb, and this one is cast out of his. Proper burial was the last honor a dynasty could give, and denying it was a recognized posthumous sentence. The chapter's harshest line is about real estate six feet deep.

world_behind.title: Dated to a death, again
world_behind.text: Verse 28 fixes the burden to the year king Ahaz died, the same dating device the block used for Isaiah's call. The block opens and closes with a king's death as its calendar, and both times the point is that the throne in view is not the one in Jerusalem.

words.text: Stringed instruments, the music of a royal court. The verse puts them in the past tense and pairs them with worms: the noise of the viols is not heard, and the bedding is maggots. Isaiah furnishes the grave with the two things a palace had most and least of.

Morning star, the light that rises just before dawn and is gone as soon as the sun is up. As a name it is the King James rendering of a Hebrew phrase, and the astronomy is the whole figure: the brightest thing in the sky, and the first to be outshone. The record's own account of a fallen angel who became the devil sits four chapters back in Jacob's sermon.

In older usage a grandson or descendant rather than a brother's son. The verse cuts off from Babylon the name, the remnant, the son, and the nephew, which is a legal sequence running from reputation to posterity. What is destroyed is not a generation but a line.

A marsh bird with a booming call, at home in standing water. Paired with pools, it turns the site of a great city into wetland. The chapter's picture of ruin is not rubble but drainage failure, which for a river city is the more humiliating end.
A broom made of twigs. God sweeps Babylon with the besom of destruction, and the domestic scale of the tool against the size of the object does the work. An empire is cleaned up the way a floor is.

phrases.term: they shall return to their lands of promise
phrases.text: The King James verse describes captives taking their captors, and the record expands it: "yea, from far unto the ends of the earth" and "they shall return to their lands of promise" (v. 2) are additions, and the plural on lands is not incidental. A colony on the far side of an ocean, reading a promise about lands of promise in the plural, is being included in a sentence that in its source concerns one land.

spans.text: they shall return to their lands of promise

phrases.text: The taunt begins with a question that assumes its own answer. Two verbs of ceasing in one line, and the second applies to a city rather than a man: the golden city ceased. Everything after this line is the elaboration of a fact already stated, which is how a lament works.

phrases.term: no feller is come up against us
phrases.text: A feller is a woodcutter. The trees of Lebanon are given a line of dialogue, and what they say is entirely practical. Isaiah's most imaginative touch in the chapter is also his most concrete: the relief at a tyrant's death is voiced by the timber he would have harvested.

Five statements beginning with I will, stacked without a pause: ascend, exalt my throne, sit upon the mount of the congregation, ascend above the heights of the clouds, be like the Most High. The grammar is the argument. Nothing in the boast asks for anything or receives anything, and verse 15 answers all five with one word: yet.

phrases.term: the remnant of those that are slain
phrases.text: The King James has the body cast out "as the raiment of those that are slain" (Isa. 14:19), clothing stripped from corpses. This reading has remnant instead of raiment, one letter's difference in an older hand, and the sense changes from a garment to the survivors. Either way the king lies unburied among the war dead; the record's version makes them people rather than possessions.

phrases.term: I will bring the Assyrian in my land
phrases.text: The King James reads "I will break the Assyrian in my land" (Isa. 14:25). This reading has bring. The difference reverses the verse's direction: the empire is not shattered in Judah, it is brought there, and only then trodden underfoot. The block has spent chapters establishing that Assyria arrives on assignment, and this variant states it once more at the end.

The block's last sentence, and the answer given to foreign envoys asking what has happened. Not a report of a victory, not a treaty, not a boast about survival. The answer is that God founded Zion, and that the poor of his people trust in it, which puts the two weakest words in the chapter, poor and trust, in its final line.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: Mercy before taunt
verses.text: Before a word is said about Babylon's king, three verses promise mercy on Jacob, a return to their own land, strangers joined to the house of Jacob, and rest from sorrow, fear, and hard bondage. The order matters. The song against the oppressor is sung by people who have already been told they are going home.

verses.label: v. 4–8
verses.title: The lament, and the trees
verses.text: The taunt opens with two things ceasing and then works outward: the staff of the wicked broken, the persecutor persecuted, the whole earth quiet and breaking into song. The last voice is the strangest and the best, cedars glad that no woodcutter is coming. Relief is registered by everything the tyrant used.

verses.label: v. 9–11
verses.title: The reception below
verses.text: Hell stirs itself to meet him, kings rise from their thrones to look, and their entire greeting is two questions about whether he has become weak like them. Then the furnishings: no music, worms for a bed. The passage is a state welcome performed by the dead, and it is entirely deflationary.

verses.label: v. 12–15
verses.title: Five I wills and one Yet
verses.text: The boast climbs by repetition, each clause reaching higher than the last, and the reply takes half a verse. Down to hell, to the sides of the pit. The chapter's whole argument about pride is contained in the ratio: five lines up, one line down, and the down is further than the up.

verses.label: v. 16–20
verses.title: Looked at closely
verses.text: Those who see him narrowly look and consider, and the questions they ask are about scale: is this the man that made the earth tremble? Then the indignity, cast out of his own grave, unburied among the slain. Other kings lie in glory in their own houses. He is the exception, and the reason given is what he did to his own land and people.

verses.label: v. 24–27
verses.title: The purpose, and the hand
verses.text: Four verses turn from Babylon to method. What God has thought will come to pass, what he has purposed will stand, and the hand stretched out over all nations cannot be turned back. The block has ended four movements with that outstretched hand as a threat. Here it is named as a purpose, which is the last thing said about it.

verses.label: v. 28–32
verses.title: One more burden, and one more answer
verses.text: A short oracle against Palestina is appended, warning them not to celebrate a broken rod too early. Then the messengers arrive with a question, and the chapter, the block, and Isaiah's part in this record end on the reply: the Lord founded Zion, and the poor trust in it.

chapter.title: The block ends where it began, on a mountain
chapter.text: Chapter 12 opened with the mountain of the Lord's house established in the top of the mountains and nations flowing to it. Chapter 24 closes with Zion founded and the poor of his people trusting in it. Between those two sentences lie thirteen chapters of judgment on everything else that claimed height.

chapter.title: Pride is given its clearest anatomy
chapter.text: Five ascending claims, each a first-person intention, and no request in any of them. The block has described pride as height, as competence, as self-crediting, and as haughtiness. Here it is shown as ambition that has stopped asking, and the answer is a single adversative.

chapter.title: Two variants change the theology of a verse each
chapter.text: Raiment to remnant at verse 19 turns stripped clothing into surviving people; break to bring at verse 25 turns the shattering of Assyria into its summoning. Both are single-word differences, and both agree with positions the block has already argued at length.

chapter.title: The record reads a second figure into the passage
chapter.text: Isaiah's subject is the king of Babylon, named as such in verse 4, and the Lucifer verses are a taunt against him. Jacob's sermon in this same book had described an angel fallen from God's presence who became the devil, and later scripture makes the identification explicit. The chapter as Nephi copied it does not, and both readings are available in it.

chapter.title: Mercy frames the judgment on both sides
chapter.text: Chapter 23 ended with an added sentence about mercy to God's people; chapter 24 opens with three verses of it. The two chapters that pronounce the heaviest sentences in the block are the ones bracketed most deliberately by promise, and one of those brackets exists only in this record.

chapter.title: The last word is about the poor
chapter.text: After empires, kings, hell, thrones, and the mount of the congregation, the block closes on the poor of his people trusting in a founded city. Nephi chose the stopping point, and the choice is consistent with everything he said in chapter 11 about why he was copying at all.

applications.title: Read the mercy before the judgment
applications.text: When a passage or a season feels like sentencing, look for the promise that precedes it, and read the two in the order they were given rather than in the order they hit you.

applications.title: Count your I wills
applications.text: Write the five things you most intend for your own life, in the same grammar. Then read them back and notice how many are requests and how many are announcements. The chapter is not against ambition; it is against ambition that has stopped asking.

applications.title: Ask the trees
applications.text: Consider what in your life would be relieved if some drive of yours stopped: your calendar, your family's evenings, your own body. The cedars are glad about a specific practice ending. Name yours.

applications.title: Look narrowly at what frightens you
applications.text: The onlookers in this chapter examine the fallen tyrant closely and find him smaller than his reputation. Take the thing currently looming over you and inspect it in detail rather than at a distance.

applications.title: Decline the early celebration
applications.text: Palestina is warned not to rejoice because one rod broke. When a difficulty lifts, resist declaring it over until you know whether what replaces it is smaller or larger.

applications.title: Give the messengers the right answer
applications.text: When someone asks what is going on with you, practice an answer in the chapter's shape: not a report on your circumstances, but a statement about what God has founded and whom it is for.

questions.text: What hard bondage would I most want rest from, and have I actually asked for it?
Who or what quietly braces when I walk into a room?
Which of my ambitions have I stopped submitting for approval because I assume the answer is yes?
If the yet came for one of my plans, would I recognize it as mercy or only as loss?
What would I want said over me, and does my present life make it likely?
Do I trust in what God has founded, or in what I have built next to it?
